## **Visualising Distribution**

## **1.1 Learning Outcome**

Some of the popular statistical graphics methods for visualising distribution includes histogram, probability density curve (pdf), boxplot, notch plot and violin plot. We will dive further into two relatively new statistical graphic methods for visualising distribution, namely ridgeline plot and raincloud plot by using ggplot2 and its extensions.

## **1.2 Getting Started**

### **1.2.1 Installing and loading the packages**

The following R packages are used in this exercise:

1.  ggridges, a ggplot2 extension designed for plotting ridgeline plots,
2.  ggdist, a ggplot2 extension desgined for visualising distribution and uncertainty,
3.  tidyverse, which has been introduced in the previous exercises,
4.  ggthemes, a ggplot extension that provides additional themes, scales, and geoms for the ggplots package, and
5.  colorspace, an R package that provides a broad toolbox for selecting individual colors or color palettes, manipulating these colors, and employing them in various kinds of visualisations.

The R packages are loaded via the following method:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pacman::p_load(ggdist, ggridges, ggthemes,
               colorspace, tidyverse)
```
:::


### **1.2.2 Data import**

The same data set from the previous exercises, *Exam_data.csv,* will be used.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
exam <- read_csv("../data/Exam_data.csv")
```
:::


## **1.3 Visualising Distribution with Ridgeline Plot**

[*Ridgeline plot*](https://www.data-to-viz.com/graph/ridgeline.html)is a data visualisation technique for revealing the distribution of a numeric value for several groups. Distribution can be represented using histograms or density plots, all aligned to the same horizontal scale and presented with a slight overlap.

Figure below is a ridgeline plot showing the distribution of English score by class.

![](images/Ridgeline plot example.png)

::: callout-note
-   Ridgeline plots make sense when the number of group to represent is medium to high. If we have less than 5 groups, dealing with other distribution plots is a better option.

-   It works well when there is a clear pattern in the result, such as if there is an obvious ranking in groups. Otherwise group will overlap with each other, leading to a messy plot with minimal insights.
:::

### **1.3.1 Plotting ridgeline graph: ggridges method**

ggridges package provides two main geom to plot gridgeline plots, they are: [`geom_ridgeline()`](https://wilkelab.org/ggridges/reference/geom_ridgeline.html) and [`geom_density_ridges()`](https://wilkelab.org/ggridges/reference/geom_density_ridges.html). The former takes height values directly to draw the ridgelines, and the latter first estimates data densities and then draws those using ridgelines.

The ridgeline plot below is plotted by using `geom_density_ridges()`.

::: panel-tabset
## The plot


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-4a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## The code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = MATHS, 
           y = CLASS)) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    bandwidth = 3.4,
    fill = lighten("#9097BB", .3),
    color = "white"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "Maths grades",
    expand = c(0, 0)
    ) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-4a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

:::

### **1.3.2 Varying fill colors along the x axis**

We can achieve the effect of varying colours along the x axis using [`geom_ridgeline_gradient()`](https://wilkelab.org/ggridges/reference/geom_ridgeline_gradient.html) or [`geom_density_ridges_gradient()`](https://wilkelab.org/ggridges/reference/geom_ridgeline_gradient.html). Both geoms work just like `geom_ridgeline()` and `geom_density_ridges()`, except that they allow for varying fill colors. However, they do not allow for alpha transparency in the fill.

::: panel-tabset
## The plot


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-4a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## The code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = MATHS, 
           y = CLASS,
           fill = stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Temp. [F]",
                       option = "C") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "Maths grades",
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-4a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

:::

### **1.3.3 Mapping the probabilities directly onto colour**

ggridges package also provides a stat function called [`stat_density_ridges()`](https://wilkelab.org/ggridges/reference/stat_density_ridges.html) that replaces [`stat_density()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_density.html) of ggplot2.

Figure below is plotted by mapping the probabilities calculated by using `stat(ecdf)` which represent the empirical cumulative density function for the distribution of Science, English, and Math scores.

::: panel-tabset
## Science plot


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = SCIENCE, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = 0.5 - abs(0.5-stat(ecdf)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient", 
                      calc_ecdf = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Tail probability",
                       direction = -1) +
  theme_ridges()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-4a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## The code


::: {.cell}


### **1.3.4 Ridgeline plots with quantile lines**

By using [`geom_density_ridges_gradient()`](https://wilkelab.org/ggridges/reference/geom_ridgeline_gradient.html), we can colour the ridgeline plot by quantile, via the calculated `stat(quantile)` aesthetic as shown in the figure below.

::: panel-tabset
## The plot


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-4a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## The code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = MATHS, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = factor(stat(quantile))
           )) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
    quantiles = 4,
    quantile_lines = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Quartiles") +
  theme_ridges()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-4a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

:::

We can also specify quantiles by cut points, such as 5% and 95% tails, by adding colours to the top and bottom quantiles.

::: panel-tabset
## The plot


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-4a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## The code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = MATHS, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = factor(stat(quantile))
           )) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
    quantiles = c(0.05, 0.95)
    ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Probability",
    values = c("#FF0000A0", "#A0A0A0A0", "#0000FFA0"),
    labels = c("(0, 0.05]", "(0.05, 0.95]", "(0.95, 1]")
  ) +
  theme_ridges()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-4a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

:::

## **1.4 Visualising Distribution with Raincloud Plot**

Raincloud Plot is a data visualisation technique that produces a half-density to a distribution plot. It can be created by using functions provided by **ggdist** and ggplot2 packages.

### **1.4.1 Plotting a Half Eye graph**

A Half-Eye graph is plotted by using [`stat_halfeye()`](https://mjskay.github.io/ggdist/reference/stat_halfeye.html) of **ggdist** package. The visualisation contains a half-density and a slab-interval.

::: panel-tabset
## The plot


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-4a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## The code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = MATHS)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-4a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

:::

::: callout-note
The slab interval is removed by setting .width = 0 and point_colour = NA.
:::

### **1.4.2 Adding the boxplot with `geom_boxplot()`**

A second geometry layer is added using [`geom_boxplot()`](https://r4va.netlify.app/chap09) of ggplot2. This produces a narrow boxplot. The width and the opacity are adjusted accordingly.

::: panel-tabset
## The plot


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-4a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## The code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = MATHS)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-4a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

:::

### **1.4.3 Adding the Dot Plots with `stat_dots()`**

The third geometry layer is added using [`stat_dots()`](https://mjskay.github.io/ggdist/reference/stat_dots.html) of ggdist package. This produces a half-dotplot, which is similar to a histogram that indicates the number of samples (number of dots) in each bin.

::: panel-tabset
## The plot


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-4a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## The code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = MATHS)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_dots(side = "left", 
            justification = 1.2, 
            binwidth = .5,
            dotsize = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-4a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

:::

### **1.4.4 Finishing touch**

[`coord_flip()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/coord_flip.html) of ggplot2 package is used to flip the raincloud chart horizontally to give it the raincloud appearance. At the same time, `theme_economist()` of ggthemes package is used to give the raincloud chart a professional look.

::: panel-tabset
## The plot


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-4a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## The code


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = MATHS)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_dots(side = "left", 
            justification = 1.2, 
            binwidth = .5,
            dotsize = 1.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_economist()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-4a_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::
